Bore
bōr
v. (to pierce; to make a hole through)
From the Saxon borian, to pierce. In the law it names the act that marked a servant who refused his freedom; in Job it names what no man can do to leviathan.

Biblical Definition

The word carries a statute that turns on love. A Hebrew servant completing his six years may go free, and if he will not, the refusal is made permanent in his flesh: “Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever” (Exodus 21:6). The reason he stays is stated in the preceding verse, and it is the only reason the law will accept: “And if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free” (Exodus 21:5). The ear is bored at the door of the house he has chosen. The second use is the LORD's challenge concerning leviathan: “Canst thou put an hook into his nose? or bore his jaw through with a thorn?” (Job 41:2). What a master may do to a willing servant, no man can do to that beast. Between the statute and the challenge lies the sentence the Psalmist speaks and the epistle to the Hebrews applies to Christ: “Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required” (Psalm 40:6). The willing servant with the bored ear is the Old Testament picture of the Son who said, Lo, I come to do thy will.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines bore as to perforate or penetrate a solid body and make a round hole.

expand to see more

BORE, v.t. [Sax. borian.] To perforate or penetrate a solid body and make a round hole.

AUL, n. A pointed instrument for piercing small holes in leather.

SERVANT, n. A person, male or female, that attends another for the purpose of performing menial offices for him.

MANUMISSION, n. The act of liberating a slave from bondage and giving him freedom.

DOOR-POST, n. The post of a door; the piece of timber on each side of a doorway.

Key Scripture

Exodus 21:6 — "Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever."

Exodus 21:5 — "And if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free:"

Job 41:2 — "Canst thou put an hook into his nose? or bore his jaw through with a thorn?"

Psalm 40:6 — "Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required."

Modern Corruption

The statute is cited as evidence that Scripture endorses chattel slavery, which ignores both the six-year release it commands and the servant's own stated love as the sole ground for staying.

expand to see more

Exodus 21 is regularly produced as proof that the Bible institutionalises slavery, and the charge collapses on the text. The law before the reader is a manumission law: six years of service and the seventh year free, without payment. What the bored ear records is not a master's power to detain but a servant's refusal to leave — a refusal the law requires him to state aloud, in his own words, before judges, naming love of master, wife and children as his reason. A statute whose default is release and whose exception requires the servant's spoken love is not the institution its critics describe.

The corruption that matters more for the church is the loss of the type. The New Testament reads the willing bondservant as a picture of Christ, and Paul takes the title for himself — doulos, bondservant of Jesus Christ — as an honour rather than a humiliation. A church that flinches from the word loses the doctrine the word carries: that the Son freely took the form of a servant, that His obedience was not extracted but offered, and that those bought with His blood are not their own. The mark in the ear was made at a door. The believer's mark was made at a cross.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ratsa (H7527), to bore or pierce; martsea (H4836), an aul; ebed (H5650), a servant; Greek doulos (G1401), a bondservant.

expand to see more

Hebrew ratsa (H7527) — to bore through, pierce; Exodus 21:6, bore his ear.

Hebrew martsea (H4836) — an aul, the piercing tool; used only in this statute and its parallel.

Hebrew ebed (H5650) — a servant, bondman; the man who says I love my master.

Hebrew karah (H3738) — to dig, open; Psalm 40:6, mine ears hast thou opened.

Greek doulos (G1401) — a bondservant; the title Paul claims in Romans 1:1.

Usage

"“His master shall bore his ear through with an aul” — the mark of a willing servant."

"“I love my master…I will not go out free” — the only accepted ground."

"“Canst thou…bore his jaw through with a thorn?” — what no man can do to leviathan."
